leaves.title: Sounds /h/, /aɪ/, and /i/
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice three sounds that are easy to mix up at first but are used constantly in everyday English words.

• /h/ as in 'hat' — a soft breath sound at the start of a word
• /aɪ/ as in 'my' — a long 'eye' sound
• /i/ as in 'we' — a short, high 'ee' sound

Listen carefully to the difference between the long /aɪ/ sound and the short /i/ sound — they're one of the most common mix-ups for beginners.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to hear and say the difference between these three sounds clearly.
commonMistakes: Don't drop the /h/ sound at the start of words like 'hat' or 'happy'.
Don't confuse the short /i/ in 'we' with the long /aɪ/ in 'my' — they are different sounds.

leaves.title: Sounds /ɪ/, /oʊ/, /s/, and /ʃ/
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice four more sounds that appear in very common everyday words.

• /ɪ/ as in 'sit' — short and relaxed
• /oʊ/ as in 'go' — a diphthong that glides from 'oh' to a small 'oo'
• /s/ as in 'say' — a hissing sound
• /ʃ/ as in 'she' — a softer 'sh' sound, with rounder lips than /s/

Pay special attention to /s/ vs. /ʃ/ — they're easy to confuse but change the meaning of a word completely.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to hear and say all four sounds clearly in real words.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse /s/ (say) and /ʃ/ (she) — /ʃ/ has rounder, more forward lips.
Don't shorten /oʊ/ into a pure 'o' — it glides into a small 'oo' sound.

leaves.title: Sounds /dʒ/, /tʃ/, and /ʃ/
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice three related consonant sounds that are easy to confuse with each other at first, but sound quite different once you know what to listen for.

• /dʒ/ as in 'job' — a voiced 'j' sound (your throat vibrates)
• /tʃ/ as in 'chair' — the unvoiced version of the same sound (no vibration)
• /ʃ/ as in 'shoe' — a soft 'sh' sound with no stop at the start

The letter 'j' and a soft 'g' are usually pronounced /dʒ/.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to tell these three sounds apart and use them correctly in common words.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse /dʒ/ (voiced, like 'job') with /tʃ/ (unvoiced, like 'chair') — feel your throat vibrate for /dʒ/ but not /tʃ/.
/ʃ/ has no stop at the start, unlike /tʃ/ which starts with a small stop.

leaves.title: Understanding number word pairs (13 vs. 30)
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn to hear and say the difference between number pairs like 13 and 30 — a mix-up that can genuinely confuse a price, an age, or an address if you get it wrong.

The rule is about stress, not spelling:

• Teen numbers (13, 14, 15...) are stressed on the second part: thir-TEEN, four-TEEN
• Tens numbers (30, 40, 50...) are stressed on the first part: THIR-ty, FOR-ty

This stress difference is the main way native speakers tell these numbers apart in fast speech — the sounds themselves are very similar.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to hear and say number pairs like 13/30, 14/40, and 15/50 without confusing them.
commonMistakes: Don't rely on the ending sound alone — in fast speech, 13 and 30 can sound similar unless you listen for the stress.
Saying a stressed 'thirTEEN' as 'THIRteen' makes it sound like 30 to a native listener.

leaves.title: Plural endings: /z/, /s/, and /ɪz/
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn that the plural -s ending isn't always pronounced the same way — it changes depending on the sound before it.

• /s/ after voiceless sounds — books, coats, tablets
• /z/ after voiced sounds — bags, phones, keys, pens
• /ɪz/ after 's', 'z', 'sh', 'ch' sounds — watches, glasses, pieces, change purses

This pattern also applies to the verb -s ending (he lives /z/, he watches /ɪz/), not just plural nouns.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to hear and produce the right plural ending sound automatically.
commonMistakes: Don't pronounce every plural -s the same way — 'bags' ends in /z/, not /s/.
Words already ending in an s/z/sh/ch sound need an extra syllable: 'watches' has two syllables, not one.

leaves.title: Sound /ð/ and sentence rhythm
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice the voiced 'th' sound /ð/ — one of the most common sounds in English function words — and start noticing English sentence rhythm.

/ð/ appears in very frequent short words:

this, that, these, those, the, they, mother

English sentences have a natural rhythm where the important words (nouns, verbs) are stressed and small words like 'this'/'the' are said quickly and lightly.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to produce /ð/ correctly and start copying natural English sentence rhythm.
examples: this, that, these, those — all start with /ð/
The mother and they are both common /ð/ words.
How much are these key chains?
commonMistakes: Don't pronounce /ð/ like /d/ or /z/ — the tongue should lightly touch the back of the top teeth.
Don't stress small words like 'the' or 'this' as heavily as the main noun in a sentence — that breaks the natural rhythm.

leaves.title: Sounds /ʊr/, /s/, and /k/
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice three sounds that come up constantly in words about money, travel, and price — plus a spelling rule that tells you how to pronounce the letter 'c'.

• /ʊr/ as in 'tourist' — euro, Europe, sure, tour
• /s/ as in 'snake' — cent, city, pence, price
• /k/ as in 'key' — coffee, Canada, credit card

The letter 'c' rule:

• c = /s/ before e, i, and y — e.g., cent, city
• c = /k/ before other letters — e.g., coffee

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to pronounce price- and travel-related words correctly, and predict how an unfamiliar word with 'c' is pronounced.
examples: A tourist visits Europe and needs euros.
Can I pay by credit card?
commonMistakes: Don't pronounce 'c' as /k/ before e/i/y — 'city' is /s/, not /k/.
'Sure' and 'tour' both use /ʊr/, even though they're spelled differently.

leaves.title: Sounds /ʌ/, /æ/, and /ə/
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice three vowel sounds that are extremely common in everyday family and people words.

• /ʌ/ as in 'up' — husband, Sunday, son, mother, brother
• /æ/ as in 'cat' — man, family, bag, thanks, that
• /ə/ as in 'computer' — woman, children, welcome, parent

/ə/ (schwa) is the most common vowel sound in English — it appears in syllables that aren't stressed, like the 'o' in 'welcome' or the 'a' in 'woman'.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to hear and produce these three vowel sounds correctly in common family and people words.
examples: My husband's brother is my mother's son.
The man and woman are my grandparents.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse /ʌ/ (husband, son) with /æ/ (man, family) — they are different mouth shapes.
Unstressed syllables usually reduce to /ə/, even if the spelling suggests a different vowel — 'woman' does not rhyme with 'man'.

leaves.title: Sounds /ɑr/ and /ɔr/, and linking
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice two r-colored vowel sounds that are easy to confuse, plus how English speakers link words together in fast speech.

• /ɑr/ as in 'car' — large, park, are, tomorrow
• /ɔr/ as in 'horse' — short, sport, orange, door

Linking: when a word ends in a consonant and the next word starts with a vowel sound, speakers often join them smoothly, e.g. 'a big‿umbrella', 'an old‿man', 'an expensive‿watch'.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to tell /ɑr/ and /ɔr/ apart and link words together more naturally when speaking.
examples: The short sport is popular here.
This is a big umbrella and an old man's coat.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse /ɑr/ (car, park) with /ɔr/ (short, door) — they use different mouth shapes.
Don't pause between a consonant and the next word's vowel sound — link them smoothly instead of saying each word separately.

leaves.title: Sounds /dʒ/ and /g/
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how the letters 'g' and 'j' relate to sound in English — a common source of confusion since the same letter can be pronounced two different ways.

• /dʒ/ as in 'jazz' — juice, vegetables, orange
• /g/ as in 'girl' — sugar, yogurt, eggs

The letter j is always /dʒ/. The letter g is sometimes /g/ (sugar) and sometimes /dʒ/ (orange) — especially before the letter 'e'.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to predict and produce the correct sound for words spelled with 'g' or 'j'.
examples: I like orange juice and vegetables.
She has eggs and yogurt with sugar.
commonMistakes: Don't assume 'g' is always /g/ — before 'e', it's often /dʒ/, as in 'orange' and 'vegetables'.
The letter 'j' is always /dʒ/, with no exceptions in common words.

leaves.title: Sounds /w/ and /v/, sentence rhythm and linking
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice two consonant sounds that are easy to confuse for many learners, plus more practice linking words smoothly in a sentence.

• /w/ as in 'witch' — want, work, when, where
• /v/ as in 'vase' — very, have, live, TV

For /w/, round your lips; for /v/, touch your top teeth to your bottom lip — they use completely different mouth positions even though they can sound similar to some learners.

Linking still matters here: 'live‿in a house', 'have‿a big family' — join the consonant to the next vowel sound smoothly.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to tell /w/ and /v/ apart and link them naturally into full sentences.
examples: I live in a very big house.
Do you want to watch TV?
We work in the same office.
commonMistakes: Don't substitute /v/ for /w/ or vice versa — 'want' and 'vant' are different sounds to a native listener.
Remember to link 'have a' and 'live in' smoothly rather than pausing between the words.

leaves.title: Sound /ɑ/ and silent consonants
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice the /ɑ/ vowel sound and learn about silent letters — letters that are written but not pronounced, which can trip up even careful readers.

/ɑ/ appears in common words like: what, Oxford, sorry, coffee

Some English words have a silent letter, e.g. in 'where', the 'h' is silent: /wɛr/. Other common examples: 'know' (silent k), 'listen' (silent t), 'half' (silent l), 'Wednesday' (silent d), 'write' (silent w).

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to produce the /ɑ/ sound correctly and recognize common silent letters instead of pronouncing every letter you see.
examples: What time is it? I'm sorry, I don't know.
commonMistakes: Don't pronounce the 'h' in 'where' — it's silent: /wɛr/, not /hwɛr/.
Don't pronounce the 'w' in 'write' or the 'k' in 'know' — both are silent letters.
